title: Collection and Presentation of Data
summary: ## Information and data

Information can be qualitative or quantitative. Qualitative information describes qualities: good, bad, beautiful, educated. Quantitative information is given in numbers: income, height, marks, population. Economics mostly uses quantitative information.
Data means quantitative information giving facts in an aggregate manner. It is also called statistical data or statistics. 'Data' is plural; the singular is 'datum'.
## Features of data (statistics)
(1) An aggregate of facts. One student's marks (95) is a single fact; the marks of the whole class are data and can be compared and analysed.
(2) Numerically expressed. Qualities such as good or ugly are attributes, not data.
(3) Affected by many causes. A rise in prices may come from lower supply, higher demand, higher taxes or higher wages.
(4) A reasonable standard of accuracy. 100% accuracy is neither possible nor desirable.
(5) Collected for a predetermined purpose.
## Importance of data in economics
(1) Economic planning: past data are used to plan the future, such as spending on primary education. Planning is based on forecasts made from statistics.
(2) National income: data on wages, rent, interest and profit are needed to work it out.

(3) Government policies: data on poverty and unemployment led to MGNREGA (100 days of wage employment). The Census, held every 10 years, showed 938 females per 1,000 males in India (848 in Haryana), which led to policies to save the girl child.
## Primary and secondary data
Primary data are collected for the first time by the investigator for the survey. The investigator collects the information; the respondent (informant) answers. They can be collected in five ways.
(1) Direct personal investigation: the investigator meets respondents personally. It is the most reliable method, but it risks personal bias and suits a small number of respondents.
(2) Indirect investigation: information is obtained from third persons who know the facts. It is used by government commissions.
(3) Through correspondents: agents in different places send information to the investigator. It is used by newspapers.
(4) Mailed questionnaire: respondents fill in a questionnaire sent by post. It is used only when respondents are literate.
(5) Schedules: field workers ask the questions and write down the answers. It is useful when respondents are illiterate.

Secondary data are collected by others earlier and used again. Published sources include newspaper and RBI reports, trade associations, annual reports, SEBI, official publications, and the UNO and World Bank. Unpublished sources include internal government reports, institutional records and students' research reports.
## Classification
Classification arranges raw (unorganised) data into classes or groups by their resemblance.

A variable can be measured by size or time, such as height, weight, distance or income. A discrete variable takes specific whole values, such as the number of children. A continuous variable can take any value in a range, such as height. An attribute cannot be measured, such as beauty, bravery, intelligence, laziness or being educated.
## Series

An individual series shows items individually. Raw data arranged in ascending or descending order is an array. A discrete series shows exact values with their frequencies, e.g. marks 30, 40, 50 with f 4, 6, 10. A continuous series shows class intervals with their frequencies, e.g. 0–10, 10–20 with f 7, 13; it may be exclusive or inclusive.
## Tabulation and diagrams
Tabulation puts classified data in rows and columns. A table has a title, captions, stubs, a body, a source and footnotes.

Diagrams present data geometrically, so they can be understood at a glance. Bar diagrams are one-dimensional: only the height of a bar matters. In a simple bar diagram the bars are of uniform width and placed at equal distances, usually vertical on a horizontal base.
Graphs show time series or frequency distributions as lines or curves, with time on the X-axis and the variable on the Y-axis.

Why is 100% accuracy in statistics neither possible nor desirable?

Data are collected from large numbers and affected by many causes, so complete accuracy is impossible and costly. A reasonable standard of accuracy, such as 90% of patients responding to a medicine, is enough for decisions.

sa: Are statistical data always quantitative? Explain.

Yes. Statistics are numerically expressed facts obtained by counting, measuring or estimating, e.g. marks or income.
Qualitative information such as good, honest or beautiful (attributes) cannot be measured, so it is not statistics.
Attributes can be used only when counted, e.g. the number of literate persons.
October 2024

or: 'Data are collected for a predetermined purpose.' Explain.

Data are collected with a definite aim in mind.
Marks of a whole class are collected to evaluate performance in mathematics; numbers admitted to colleges are collected to judge higher education in a city.
Data without a purpose are useless and may be misleading.

sa: Explain 'statistics are an aggregate of facts' with an example.

A single fact is not statistics: 'a student scored 95 in mathematics' cannot be analysed.
The marks of all 18 students of the class are statistics, because we can see how many scored above 90, how many failed, and so on.
So only an aggregate of facts allows comparison and analysis.

Distinguish between a variable and an attribute with examples.

A variable can be measured in size or time, e.g. height, weight, income or distance. It may be discrete (number of children) or continuous (height).
An attribute is a quality that cannot be measured, e.g. beauty, bravery, intelligence or laziness. It can only be counted for limited study.

Discrete series: exact values are shown with their frequencies, e.g. marks 30, 40, 50, 60 with 4, 6, 10, 20 students.

la: What are primary data? Explain any two methods of collecting primary data.

Primary data are collected for the first time by the investigator for the purpose of the survey.
(1) Direct personal investigation: the investigator personally meets the respondents and collects the information. It is the most reliable and suits a small area, but it may be affected by the investigator's bias.
(2) Mailed questionnaire: a well-structured questionnaire is posted to respondents, who fill it in and return it. It is cheap and covers a wide area but works only with literate respondents.
Other methods: indirect investigation, correspondents and schedules.
Explain (a) direct personal investigation and (b) indirect investigation.

(a) Direct personal investigation: the investigator goes to the respondents and collects the data personally. The data are original and most reliable, and the investigator can cross-check. But it is costly and slow and suits a small area, and the investigator's bias may creep in.
(b) Indirect investigation: information is collected from third persons who are expected to know the facts about the person or matter under study, e.g. witnesses. It is used by government commissions and enquiry committees, covers a wide field and suits cases where people would not answer directly. Its accuracy depends on the third persons.
Explain the importance of data in (a) economic planning and (b) framing government policies.

(a) Economic planning: past data are the base for future plans. To plan spending on primary education, data on past enrolment and expenditure are needed. To forecast growth in per-capita income, data on population and national income are needed.
(b) Government policies: data on poverty and unemployment led to MGNREGA, guaranteeing 100 days of wage employment. Census data showing 938 females per 1,000 males (848 in Haryana) led to policies to save the girl child. Data also guide fiscal and monetary policy.

(1) An aggregate of facts — a single fact is not statistics.
(2) Numerically expressed — qualities are not statistics.
(3) Affected by many causes — prices rise from many factors.
(4) A reasonable standard of accuracy — 100% accuracy is neither possible nor desirable.
(5) Collected for a predetermined purpose.
(6) Placed in relation to each other, so they can be compared.
